what_its_for: Carboplatin is a chemotherapy medicine used to treat certain types of cancer, most commonly ovarian cancer. It works by damaging the DNA inside cancer cells, which stops them from growing and multiplying. Your doctor may also use it to treat lung, head and neck, bladder, or other cancers.
how_to_take: Carboplatin is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion, meaning it is put directly into your vein through a needle or a port. A nurse or doctor will give you this medicine at a hospital, clinic, or infusion center. You will NOT take this medicine as a pill at home. Each infusion usually takes about 15 minutes to 1 hour. Do not try to give this medicine to yourself at home.
dosing: Your dose is carefully calculated by your doctor based on your kidney function, your weight or body surface area, and the type of cancer being treated. Most patients receive carboplatin once every 3 to 4 weeks as part of a treatment cycle. Never change your dose or schedule on your own. Always follow your cancer care team's instructions exactly.
missed_dose: Because carboplatin is given at a clinic or hospital by a healthcare professional, it is very important to keep all of your scheduled appointments. If you need to miss or reschedule an appointment, call your doctor or nurse as soon as possible so they can find the best time to reschedule your treatment. Do not skip doses without talking to your care team first.
storage: You will not store carboplatin at home since it is prepared and given by healthcare professionals. If you are ever given any supplies related to your treatment to take home, store them exactly as your pharmacist or nurse instructs. Keep all cancer medicines away from children and pets.
what_to_avoid: Avoid contact with people who are sick or have infections, since carboplatin lowers your ability to fight germs. Avoid crowds and wash your hands often. Do not get any live vaccines (such as the nasal flu spray) without asking your doctor first. Avoid alcohol unless your doctor says it is okay. Avoid pregnancy during treatment, as carboplatin can harm an unborn baby. Use reliable birth control during treatment and for some time after. Breastfeeding is not recommended while receiving carboplatin.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience any of the following: fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher, chills, or signs of infection; unusual bruising or bleeding; severe nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea that you cannot control; blood in your urine or stool; difficulty breathing or chest pain; swelling of the face, lips, or throat (signs of a serious allergic reaction); extreme tiredness or weakness; ringing in your ears or sudden hearing changes; numbness, tingling, or pain in your hands or feet; or any new or worsening symptoms that concern you.
when_it_works: Carboplatin does not work overnight. It works over time as part of your full treatment plan, which may include several cycles of chemotherapy. Some patients may notice improvements after a few treatment cycles, but your doctor will check how well the medicine is working through blood tests, scans, or other tests. Be patient and keep all follow-up appointments.
special_populations: Kidney problems: Carboplatin is removed from your body by your kidneys. If your kidneys do not work well, your doctor will carefully adjust your dose to keep you safe. Older adults: Older patients may be more sensitive to side effects such as low blood counts and kidney changes, so your doctor will monitor you closely. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Carboplatin can harm an unborn baby and should not be used during pregnancy. Do not breastfeed while receiving this medicine. Talk to your doctor about safe birth control options. Children: Carboplatin is sometimes used in children for certain cancers, but the dose and schedule will be carefully chosen by a specialist based on the child's weight and health.
